# Graph Connectivity and Resilience

"Is this network connected?" is a yes/no question. "**What breaks it?**" is the useful one, and it has
precise graph-theoretic answers. Both lab-5 applications in
[[discrete-mathematics-laboratories]] are built around turning those answers into a failure
simulation.

## The structural vocabulary

| Object | Definition | Operational meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Bridge** | edge whose removal disconnects the graph | a single link with no redundancy |
| **Articulation point** | vertex whose removal disconnects the graph | a single node whose loss splits the network |
| **Edge connectivity κ′(G)** | minimum edges to cut | how many simultaneous link failures survive |
| **Biconnected component** | maximal subgraph with no articulation point | a region that tolerates any one node loss |

**Tarjan's algorithm** finds bridges and articulation points in one DFS pass by tracking each
vertex's discovery time and the lowest discovery time reachable from its subtree — the `low` value.
An edge `(u,v)` is a bridge when `low[v] > disc[u]`; no cross-edge climbs back past `u`.

## The honest bound

The lab does not pretend to compute κ′(G) properly, and says so in the source:

> "// For this dataset: if any bridge exists, κ'(G) = 1; otherwise treat as 2 (a conservative
> placeholder — a full Stoer-Wagner cut is out of scope)."
> — Discrete-Mathematics-Laboratories/lab5_GraphTheory/SentinelNet/sn-algo.js, 2026-06-09

That is a correct lower-bound argument stated as a limitation rather than dressed up as a result —
the pattern is [[provenance-and-limits-stated-inline]].

## Two applications of the same machinery

**SentinelNet** (Iberian monitoring grid) also computes bipartiteness by 2-colouring, clustering
coefficient, diameter and radius, Euler status with a greedy Chinese-Postman pairing, Hierholzer's
tour construction, and both Prim and Kruskal spanning trees (Kruskal over a path-halving union-find —
see [[ackermann-and-primitive-recursion]] for why that is effectively constant time). BFS and DFS are
rendered as **replayable step-frames**, not as final answers.

**Q-HYDRO Wrocław** (25-node Lower-Silesia gravimeter mesh) uses the same primitives for a
**stackable node-failure simulation**: fail nodes cumulatively, recompute connectivity, and propose
the cheapest link augmentation that repairs it by a greedy min-cost rule. It also checks planarity via
the Euler bound `E ≤ 3V − 6` — a necessary condition, not a planarity test, which the app is careful
about. Its `data.js` is a single source of truth with every displayed figure recomputed on load
rather than hard-coded.

## Finding: not actually Christofides

`sn-algo.js` names a function `tspChristofides`, but it matches odd-degree vertices **greedily**
instead of by minimum-weight perfect matching. The 1.5-approximation guarantee depends entirely on
that matching being optimal, so **the guarantee does not hold**. It should be read as a
*Christofides-shaped heuristic*. Detail on [[shortest-path-algorithm-family]]. `confidence: high` —
read from source. **TODO:** whether this was known at the time is unrecorded.
